Mina / team — answers and evidence notes below (technical summary first, then evidence links/attachments). I focused on the two deployment models Kestrel cares about: 1) Private-hosted (customer VPC) and 2) On-prem / airgapped.

1) Operator actions and required egress (day-to-day operations)
- Normal maintenance and operator tasks (logs review, scaling, health checks) do NOT require outbound internet by default. All operator tooling runs over customer-controlled management plane (bastion/jump hosts, VPN, or VPC peering) to the customer VPC where the runtime is deployed.
- Optionally, customers can enable a customer-managed telemetry forwarder. If disabled, no telemetry leaves the customer environment. By default telemetry is off for Private and Off by default for On-prem.
- Emergency support: outbound egress may be required only if the customer authorizes a remote debug window. Those windows are timeboxed, logged, and require two-person approval (customer admin + Redwood on-call).

2) Operator account constraints and separation
- Operator roles are split: Operator (day-to-day ops), Admin (configuration/installation), and Security Auditor (read-only). RBAC enforced via our control plane plus integrations with customer IdP (SAML/OIDC).
- For Private (VPC) deployments, operator accounts can be constrained to customer-managed control plane endpoints (customer IdP and customer-managed bastion). Operators do not need Redwood-managed public endpoints to operate.
- For On-prem / airgap, operators run from within the customer's network only; no Redwood cloud console access is required except via an approved VPN jump.
- MFA and hardware-backed keys (FIDO2 / YubiKey) are recommended and supported.

3) Signed attestation and airgap/patch process
- We use cryptographic artifact signing for all runtime binaries and container images. Artifact signing keys are held in Redwood's KMS; for airgap customers we provide an option to accept images signed by Redwood or to transfer signing keys to a customer-managed HSM under an agreed key-escrow process.
- Update workflow (airgap): vendor publishes signed artifact bundle -> customer downloads via secured channel or via physical media -> customer verifies signatures using public keys we provide -> operator performs offline install. We provide a step-by-step runbook for verification and rollback.
- For attestation: we supply a templated signed attestation (signed by our security lead) that certifies the build IDs and artifact checksums shipped for the customer. We can sign a bespoke attestation per release upon purchase (usually post-MSA/attachment).

4) Network controls and egress hardening
- All outbound network egress is configurable. Recommended pattern: deploy a single customer-controlled egress gateway for optional outbound-only artifact retrieval. This gateway is the only host allowed to reach external artifact mirrors in our recommended architecture.
- DNS, proxy, and IP allowlist controls supported. Customers can route update checks to an internal mirror or our S3-compatible endpoint over TLS with client certs.
- By default, no analytics or usage data will be sent to Redwood's cloud in Private/On-prem deployments unless explicitly opted-in and signed off by the customer.

5) Evidence and artifacts (attached)
- redwood_operator_runbook_v2.pdf — step-by-step install / maintenance for airgap and private VPC (includes verification commands, checksum verification, rollback steps).
- soc2_control_map.csv — mapping of our SOC2 controls to customer evidence collection points relevant for operator access and change management.
- signed_attestation_kestrel.pdf — templated attestation; we can sign with build IDs after you confirm the release.

Notes / open items:
- If Kestrel requires HSM custody of signing keys, we'll need a short PKI/key-escrow engagement (standard T&C).
- For emergency remote debug we require signed approval and will provide a per-session audit trail.

Attaching the runbook and SOC2 mapping for your package. Let me know if you want a redline to the attestation language.
